demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette: John, a 55-year-old African man and painter, has been struggling with intense emotional distress since his wife's unexpected death six months ago. John's life was forever altered when he received the devastating news that his beloved spouse had passed away due to sudden cardiac arrest while at work. Since then, John finds himself hyper-vigilant in various situations. The sound of an ambulance siren, a common occurrence in his neighborhood, immediately triggers a surge of anxiety and fear, making him feel as though he is back on the day when everything changed. This reaction has significantly impacted his ability to sleep peacefully at night. He often finds himself unable to relax, constantly aware that danger could lurk just beyond his home's threshold. The constant tension in his body and the feeling of being perpetually on guard have made it difficult for him to fully engage with everyday activities. John's triggers are not limited to external stimuli; they also stem from his workplace environment. As a painter, he frequently encounters conversations about accidents and loss, which invariably lead to painful recollections of his wife's passing. These discussions evoke such intense grief that he often feels overwhelmed by emotions, even without clear visual memories of the event itself. These triggers have intensified John's negative appraisals about himself and his life. He has come to believe that since losing his wife, he no longer understands who he is or what purpose he serves. This sense of identity loss exacerbates his feelings of isolation from others; he often feels as though he cannot connect with people in the same way anymore because they do not fully comprehend the depths of his grief. The intensity of these negative appraisals has created a feedback loop that further escalates John's threat perceptions and memories. His belief that life is irreparably destroyed by trauma makes him hyper-aware of potential dangers, even when he is at home. This heightened sense of alertness keeps his body in a constant state of readiness for danger, which in turn reinforces the negative appraisals about himself and his future. Conversely, John's distressing memories often bring on waves of grief that are so intense they can be experienced without any clear visual recollections. The emotional intensity of these moments is overwhelming, causing him to feel as though he is reliving the trauma all over again. This experience further isolates him from others and deepens his sense of loss. The interplay between John's memories and triggers has created a complex web of reactions that perpetuate each other. Each time he hears an ambulance siren or engages in conversations about loss, it brings back the emotional pain of losing his wife. These reminders intensify his negative appraisals and heighten his sense of threat. Over the past months, John's work performance has suffered as these symptoms have grown more severe. He often avoids social gatherings and struggles to maintain connections with colleagues due to his heightened anxiety and grief. His inability to cope effectively has strained his relationships with family members, leaving him feeling increasingly isolated. What finally brought John to seek help was the realization that he could no longer bear the burden of these overwhelming emotions alone. While he hopes for a return to some sense of normalcy, what frightens him most is the fear of never finding peace and being trapped in this cycle of grief and anxiety forever.
